newsitem.title: USA: Miami budget monitoring provision is key--analyst.
newsitem.headline: Miami budget monitoring provision is key--analyst.

text.p: The approval of Miami's latest deficit-closing plan is an important "first benchmark" that contains key monitoring provision set by the state-appointed oversight board, a municipal bond rating analyst said Tuesday.
The oversight board approved the city's revised budget on Monday after rejecting previous revenue estimates as unrealistic.

The revised plan uses one-time payments and proceeds from land sales and leases to help close the city's $68 milion budget gap and build $4 million in cash reserves by the end of fiscal 1997 on Sept 30.

"We don't know to a large extent whether some of these revenues will come in on a timely basis or whether or not they'll come in in the amounts expected," said John Incorvaia, vice president at Moody's Investors Service, which rates Miami's general obligation debt Ba1.

However, Incorvaia said, "We get a lot of comfort from the fact that the city has to provide cash flow (data) and a report to the board on a monthly basis showing how expected revenues and expense reductions are performing related to the recovery plan."
"This is a developing plan and it has to be something that's monitored closely," Incorvaia said.
He noted that the city met the oversight board's requirement that at least 60 percent of receurring costs for fiscal 1997 be covered with recurring revenues.

"Those are the positives," Incorvaia said. "They've reached the first benchmark. You have an independent state commission who is actually saying, 'This is a plan we can start to work with.' We realize this is only the beginning. This is the starting point. Now the real work begins."

That work will include eliminating the structural budget problems that pushed Miami into the red to begin with. By April 15, the city must submit to the oversight board a five-year budget that covers 100 percent of recurring expenses with recurring revenues.
Gov. Lawton Chiles appointed the oversight board to guide Miami to fiscal solvency after the city discovered a $68 million deficit in the $275 million budget for the fiscal year that began Oct. 1.
Rating analysts at Standard & Poor's Copr were not immediately available for comment on the new budget, and Fitch Investors Service Inc does not rate City of Miami debt.
